{
  "analyses": [
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1145-1247715-1247720",
      "title": "Temporal profiles of queries",
      "research_question": "Can temporal profiles derived from the timestamps of retrieved documents characterize a query's temporal dependence, classify temporal query types, and improve prediction of retrieval effectiveness?",
      "methodology": "The authors construct a probability distribution over dates for each query from the timestamps and retrieval scores of its top-ranked documents, then derive features including temporal KL divergence, autocorrelation, kurtosis, and burst-model statistics. They evaluate these features on TREC news collections and an ISP web-search log, manually defining atemporal, temporally unambiguous, and temporally ambiguous query classes. Decision trees with stratified cross-validation are used for temporal classification, while Spearman correlation, linear/ridge regression, and neural networks are used to predict average precision from temporal features alone or combined with content clarity.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Temporal-profile features distinguish temporal query classes substantially better than majority-class baselines on several evaluated collections.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7. Automatic Classification of Queries into Temporal Types"
        },
        {
          "finding": "On the TREC Novelty queries, classification accuracy was 0.56 for the majority baseline, 0.62 with content clarity, 0.68 with temporal features, and 0.70 when temporal features and content clarity were combined.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7.1 Results Automatically Classifying Novelty Queries"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For distinguishing temporally ambiguous from atemporal ad-hoc queries, combining temporal and content features achieved 0.73 accuracy on both the AP and WSJ collections, compared with majority baselines of 0.54 and 0.66 respectively.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7.2 Ad hoc Queries: Temporally Ambiguous and Atemporal"
        },
        {
          "finding": "In three-way classification, temporal features reached 0.75 accuracy on the search-log data versus a 0.27 majority baseline, while results were weaker on WSJ, showing that effectiveness varies substantially by collection.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "7.3 Temporally Unambiguous, Temporally Ambiguous, and Atemporal Queries"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Temporal features used alone were generally weak predictors of average precision, but combining them with content clarity produced substantially stronger held-out correlations than either feature family alone.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "8.4-8.5 Precision Prediction Results"
        },
        {
          "finding": "For linear regression, held-out correlation with average precision rose to 0.52 on AP and 0.60 on WSJ when temporal and content features were combined, versus 0.21 and 0.36 respectively for content clarity alone.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "8.5 Results of Linear Regression of Features against Average Precision"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The study explicitly cautions that its temporal-profile estimator was evaluated on collections with approximately uniform document distributions over time and may not transfer directly to temporally nonuniform collections.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "11. Discussion"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The temporal-profile estimator was developed and evaluated primarily on collections with approximately uniform temporal document distributions, while adapting it to nonuniform collections was left open.",
        "The temporal classes were motivated partly by the authors' intuition about useful forms of disambiguation rather than by a user-centered taxonomy validated through deployment.",
        "No user study or deployed search experiment evaluated whether the proposed temporal feedback and visualization actually improve user satisfaction or task completion.",
        "Some three-class experiments relied on manually constructed temporally unambiguous queries because the natural TREC ad-hoc query sets did not contain all three classes.",
        "The ISP search-log corpus itself was not released, although a manually constructed query set for the log experiments was made public.",
        "The temporal model primarily uses document timestamps and does not exploit temporal expressions contained inside document text."
      ],

        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "temporal_features_improve_query_classification": 0.98,

        "three_temporal_query_classes_are_operationally_distinguishable": 0.94,
        "performance_varies_by_collection": 0.98,
        "uniform_temporal_distribution_is_a_transfer_limit": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "A query's retrieved-document timeline can be represented as a probability distribution over dates.",
        "The paper distinguishes atemporal, temporally unambiguous, and temporally ambiguous queries.",
        "Temporal KL divergence measures how much a query's time distribution differs from the collection-wide temporal distribution.",
        "Burst features are used to characterize event-like structure in retrieved-document timelines.",
        "Decision-tree classifiers use temporal features to assign queries to temporal classes.",
        "Temporal features outperform the majority baseline in the reported classification experiments.",
        "Most temporal features are weak predictors of average precision when considered individually.",
        "Combining temporal and content features improves average-precision prediction relative to using either group alone.",
        "Queries predicted to have poor retrieval quality are proposed as candidates for additional feedback or temporal disambiguation.",
        "The authors identify nonuniform temporal document distributions and the absence of user studies as unresolved issues."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://841.io/doc/temporal-profiles-journal.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "doi-10-1145-1571941-1572085",
      "title": "Improving search relevance for implicitly temporal queries",
      "research_question": "Can frequency patterns of year-qualified query variants reveal implicit temporal intent and be used to improve ranking for queries whose desired results depend on a year that the user did not explicitly specify?",
      "methodology": "The paper mines aggregate query-log frequencies to identify base queries that are repeatedly qualified with different years, without using click, user, or session information. It defines a year-qualified weight and a temporal-ambiguity score measuring how strongly year qualifications dominate other query qualifications. The inferred year distribution and ambiguity score are then used to modify a commercial search engine's document scores according to years appearing in document fields. Evaluation uses 670 web queries with editorial relevance judgments and reports DCG@5 across temporal-ambiguity ranges.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "The query-log analysis estimated that more than 7% of queries belong to the implicitly year-qualified category considered by the paper.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "1. Introduction"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The proposed mining algorithm can infer implicit temporal intent solely from frequencies of base queries and their year-qualified variants, without click or session data.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "2. Mining Algorithm"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Baseline DCG@5 decreased monotonically as queries became more strongly associated with implicit temporal intent, indicating that the commercial search engine performed worse on the most temporally specific queries in this evaluation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Temporal reordering produced little or negative change for low-ambiguity-score groups but improved the highest temporal-intent group from 7.02 to 7.07 DCG@5, a reported 0.84% statistically significant improvement.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. Evaluation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The effectiveness of temporal reordering increased as the estimated confidence that a query had implicit temporal intent increased.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3. Evaluation"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The method addresses only implicitly year-qualified queries and therefore covers a narrow subset of possible temporal information needs.",
        "The evaluation uses a proprietary query log and a commercial search engine, which limits independent reproduction.",
        "The reordering experiment uses parameters tied to the evaluation period, including a Gaussian centered on the year 2008.",
        "The statistically significant ranking improvement is confined to the group with the strongest inferred temporal intent, while lower-confidence groups show negligible or negative changes.",
        "The method infers temporal intent from aggregate qualification behavior and does not determine the intent of an individual user issuing an ambiguous base query.",
        "The study does not address permissions, source versioning, or changing validity of retrieved evidence beyond year-oriented relevance."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": false,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "query_logs_expose_implicit_year_intent": 0.98,
        "strong_temporal_intent_correlates_with_lower_baseline_relevance": 0.97,
        "temporal_reordering_helps_high_confidence_temporal_queries": 0.99,
        "benefit_is_not_uniform_across_queries": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The paper defines an implicitly year-qualified query as one that omits a year even though the user's intent may concern a particular year.",
        "A base query is treated as implicitly year qualified when it appears with at least two distinct year qualifications in the query log.",
        "The mining procedure uses query-frequency information rather than user, click, or session data.",
        "Temporal ambiguity is estimated from the share of a query's qualifications that are years.",
        "The ambiguity measure can also be interpreted as confidence that a query carries implicit temporal intent.",
        "The reranking method boosts documents containing years that are strongly associated with the query.",
        "The evaluation contains 670 web queries with graded editorial relevance judgments.",
        "Baseline DCG@5 is lower for queries with stronger inferred temporal intent.",
        "The largest reported reordering benefit occurs for the least temporally ambiguous query group.",
        "Only the highest temporal-intent group's improvement is reported as statistically significant."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/user/rosie/www/papers/yqq.pdf",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2403.10081",
      "title": "DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Information Needs of Large Language Models",
      "research_question": "Can dynamic RAG improve knowledge-intensive generation by deciding both when to retrieve and what to retrieve from the LLM's real-time information needs rather than from fixed retrieval schedules or only the most recent generated text?",
      "methodology": "DRAGIN combines Real-time Information Needs Detection (RIND), which scores generated tokens using uncertainty, semantic importance, and influence on later tokens, with Query Formulation based on Self-attention (QFS), which selects information-relevant tokens from the broader generation context for retrieval. The framework is training-free and is evaluated with multiple LLMs on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, StrategyQA, and IIRC using Wikipedia passages and primarily BM25 retrieval. Comparisons include no-RAG, single-round RAG, fixed-length retrieval, fixed-sentence retrieval, and FLARE, with ablations isolating retrieval timing and query formulation.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "DRAGIN achieved the strongest overall performance across most evaluated LLM and dataset combinations, with especially pronounced gains on multi-hop QA tasks.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Overall Results of DRAGIN and Baselines"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Fixed-interval and fixed-sentence dynamic retrieval did not consistently outperform single-round RAG, supporting the claim that retrieving at an inappropriate generation point can be unhelpful.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Overall Results of DRAGIN and Baselines"
        },
        {
          "finding": "When query formulation was held fixed, the RIND retrieval-timing strategy outperformed the timing strategies of FLARE, fixed-length RAG, and fixed-sentence RAG on the IIRC experiments.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Timing of Retrieval"
        },
        {
          "finding": "When retrieval timing was held to RIND, QFS outperformed query formulations based on the last sentence, local token windows, FLARE's filtered sentence, and the complete generation context on HotpotQA.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.4 Query Formulation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "DRAGIN required fewer retrieval calls than fixed-length and fixed-sentence RAG in the reported efficiency comparison, although FLARE generally made the fewest retrieval calls.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Efficiency"
        },
        {
          "finding": "HotpotQA performance remained relatively stable over a broad range of RIND thresholds, while the threshold controlled how frequently retrieval was activated.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Timing of Retrieval"
        },
        {
          "finding": "BM25 outperformed the SGPT dense retriever in all three reported DRAGIN retriever comparisons on 2WikiMultihopQA, HotpotQA, and IIRC.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.5 Impact of Retriever"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "RIND and QFS require access to Transformer self-attention information, making the method unusable with APIs that do not expose the required internals.",
        "The experiments focus on four knowledge-intensive QA and reasoning benchmarks rather than long-lived workplace communication or heterogeneous enterprise evidence.",
        "The external corpus is Wikipedia segmented into fixed-size passages, so document permissions, revisions, source versions, and enterprise access-control constraints are not modeled.",
        "Retrieval stopping is driven by repeated information-need detection rather than an explicit global evidence-completeness criterion.",
        "The evaluation primarily measures answer correctness and retrieval-call counts rather than end-to-end monetary cost, temporal validity, or evidence provenance."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "dynamic_information_need_timing_improves_generation": 0.97,
        "self_attention_query_formulation_improves_retrieval_queries": 0.98,
        "fixed_retrieval_schedules_can_underperform_single_round_rag": 0.98,
        "dragin_reduces_calls_relative_to_fixed_dynamic_rag": 0.96,
        "self_attention_access_limits_api_applicability": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "DRAGIN makes separate decisions about when retrieval is needed and what query should be issued.",
        "RIND uses generation uncertainty together with token importance and influence to detect information needs.",
        "QFS uses self-attention over the generation context to choose tokens for the retrieval query.",
        "The framework does not require additional model training or fine-tuning.",
        "The evaluation covers four knowledge-intensive generation benchmarks.",
        "Single-round RAG consistently improves over direct generation in the reported experiments.",
        "Fixed-rule dynamic retrieval does not consistently improve over single-round retrieval.",
        "DRAGIN's retrieval-timing method performs better than the compared timing strategies in the timing ablation.",
        "QFS performs better than the compared query-formulation strategies in the query ablation.",
        "The full generated context is not necessarily an optimal retrieval query because it can contain redundant information.",
        "DRAGIN usually makes fewer retrieval calls than fixed-length and fixed-sentence dynamic RAG.",
        "The authors released code, data, and models for the work.",
        "The method cannot directly support APIs that hide the self-attention scores it needs."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2403.10081",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2606.29090",
      "title": "AB-RAG: Adaptive Budgeted Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Reliable Question Answering",
      "research_question": "Can a training-free RAG system use answer confidence to decide when to stop, when to retrieve more evidence, and how to bound retrieval cost while remaining usable with both open-weight models and closed APIs?",
      "methodology": "AB-RAG begins with a fixed initial retrieval depth, generates an answer, and estimates confidence from model certainty, answer-evidence embedding similarity, and variance in reranker scores. If confidence exceeds a threshold the system stops; otherwise it increases retrieval depth and repeats until confidence is sufficient or a maximum iteration budget is exhausted. Open models use token probabilities for model certainty, while models without log-probabilities use self-consistency over repeated samples. The framework is evaluated with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, Llama-3.2-3B, and Claude Haiku on pooled-corpus HotpotQA and TriviaQA experiments using EM, F1, retrieval metrics, iteration counts, and AUROC of confidence against correctness.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "AB-RAG implements an explicit retrieve-or-stop loop: answers above the confidence threshold return immediately, while low-confidence answers trigger deeper retrieval until either the threshold or the retrieval budget is reached.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "III-E The Adaptive Budgeted Loop"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The combined confidence estimator separated correct from incorrect answers on every evaluated backbone, with reported AUROC values from 0.600 to 0.733 in the static-versus-adaptive comparison.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V-B and V-C"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Adaptive retrieval improved Exact Match for Llama-3.2-3B on HotpotQA from 39.5 to 45.0 and for Claude Haiku on TriviaQA from 35.5 to 40.0, but produced no EM gain for the small Qwen model.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V-B Static RAG versus AB-RAG Across Backbones"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Model certainty was the strongest individual confidence signal, while answer-evidence cosine similarity was weak or worse than chance for short-answer QA.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V-E Signal Ablation and Diagnostics"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The original interpretation of reranker-score variance was empirically reversed: treating high variance as a penalty produced AUROC 0.427, while treating it as a reward raised AUROC to 0.573.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V-E Signal Ablation and Diagnostics"
        },
        {
          "finding": "On Claude Haiku with TriviaQA, high-confidence answers had 57.6% Exact Match while the low-confidence group had 0%, providing the strongest reported selective-prediction separation.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V-C Confidence Predicts Correctness"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The value of adaptive retrieval depends on the backbone's ability to improve when given additional evidence; the smallest tested model largely stopped after one round and did not benefit in Exact Match.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "V-B Static RAG versus AB-RAG Across Backbones"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "The open-retrieval corpora contain only a few thousand pooled passages rather than a full Wikipedia- or web-scale collection.",
        "The main evaluation uses moderate samples of 500 HotpotQA questions and 200 TriviaQA questions.",
        "Exact Match penalizes substantively correct but verbose answers, particularly for the closed model.",
        "The closed-model self-consistency proxy uses only three samples, and increasing this number could improve confidence estimation at additional cost.",
        "The three confidence-signal weights are manually specified rather than learned.",
        "The proposed answer-evidence cosine-similarity grounding signal fails on short-answer QA.",
        "Latency of extra adaptive retrieval rounds is not comprehensively characterized.",
        "Evaluation is limited to QA and does not include long-form generation, enterprise permissions, evidence versions, or temporal-validity constraints.",
        "No externally linked source-code repository is identified in the paper text that was read."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": false,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "confidence_can_drive_bounded_retrieve_or_stop_decisions": 0.99,
        "confidence_predicts_correctness_across_tested_backbones": 0.97,
        "adaptive_accuracy_gain_depends_on_backbone": 0.99,
        "answer_evidence_cosine_signal_fails_for_short_answers": 0.99,
        "reranker_variance_should_be_rewarded_not_penalized": 0.99,
        "evaluation_scale_limits_external_validity": 0.98
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "AB-RAG retrieves more evidence only when its current answer confidence is below a threshold.",
        "The adaptive loop stops when confidence is sufficient or when the maximum iteration budget is exhausted.",
        "The final estimator combines model certainty, answer-evidence similarity, and reranker-score variance.",
        "Closed models can substitute self-consistency for unavailable token probabilities.",
        "The reported adaptive policy uses a confidence threshold of 0.6 and a maximum of three iterations.",
        "Confidence separates correct from incorrect answers on all evaluated model backbones.",
        "Adaptive retrieval does not improve Exact Match on the smallest evaluated model.",
        "The largest reported adaptive gains occur on the mid-sized open model and on the closed model's TriviaQA evaluation.",
        "Model certainty is the strongest of the three individual confidence signals.",
        "Answer-evidence embedding similarity is not a useful correctness predictor for these short-answer tasks.",
        "The reranker-variance signal initially had the wrong sign and improved after its interpretation was reversed.",
        "The authors identify pooled corpora, moderate question counts, Exact Match behavior, and limited self-consistency sampling as threats to validity."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2606.29090",
      "access": "full_text"
    },
    {
      "paper_id": "2606.29959",
      "title": "Know Before You Fetch: Calibrated Retrieval-Budget Allocation for Retrieval-Augmented Generation",
      "research_question": "Can calibrated estimates of closed-book correctness be used before retrieval to allocate zero, compact, or full retrieval budgets per query, while also supporting abstention and explicitly accounting for retrieval calls, passage tokens, and latency?",
      "methodology": "The paper constructs per-query outcome tables containing closed-book, top-1-retrieval, and top-5-retrieval answers and correctness labels, then calibrates uncertainty signals such as sequence log-probability and TARG prefix statistics into probabilities of closed-book correctness. A binary gate selects between no retrieval and top-5 retrieval, while a graded policy uses two thresholds to select zero, one, or five passages. Diagnostic experiments use out-of-fold calibration, while deployment experiments fit calibration on train data, choose thresholds on validation data, and evaluate once on test data. Experiments cover TriviaQA, Natural Questions, and MS MARCO across multiple Qwen and Llama model sizes and report accuracy, multiple budget-frontier AUCs, AUROC, ECE, Brier score, NLL, risk-coverage behavior, retrieval harm, and measured latency.",
      "key_findings": [
        {
          "finding": "Logistic calibration substantially improved probability quality without materially changing the underlying ranking signal; for example, sequence-log-probability ECE on Natural Questions fell from 0.643 before calibration to 0.009 after calibration.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.1 Calibration Quality"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Graded zero/one/five-passage allocation improved full-context and passage-budget frontiers but produced essentially no improvement in retrieval-call frontier AUC because a one-passage retrieval still incurs a retrieval call.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.2 Graded Budget Allocation"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The amount of retrieval that can safely be skipped grows with reader capability: on TriviaQA, the retrieval rate needed to match always-RAG fell from 99.5% for Qwen3-1.7B to 46.0% for Qwen3-32B.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.3 Scaling, Family Transfer, and Difficulty Regimes"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Validation-selected thresholds on TriviaQA approached always-RAG accuracy while retrieving for roughly two-thirds of queries, whereas Natural Questions and MS MARCO selected retrieval for about 97-99% of queries because their closed-book headroom was low.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.4 Held-out Deployment Thresholds"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Using confidence for the answer actually returned improved selective-prediction accuracy on TriviaQA and Natural Questions, but did not outperform naive closed-book confidence on MS MARCO.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.5 Selective RAG and Abstention"
        },
        {
          "finding": "A closed-book gating probe is itself a generation cost, so adaptive retrieval is not automatically faster: at a matched-accuracy operating point Qwen3-8B gating was slower than always-RAG, while Qwen3-32B gating was faster.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "5.6 Measured Cost Regimes"
        },
        {
          "finding": "Retriever quality strongly constrains the attainable answer accuracy; confidence-based gating cannot compensate for a sufficiently noisy retriever when maximum correctness is the objective.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "6.2 Retriever Quality and Corpus Scale"
        },
        {
          "finding": "The method explicitly supports abstention as a fourth action when confidence in the selected answer remains too low.",
          "evidence_type": "supported",
          "section": "3.4 Selective RAG"
        }
      ],
      "limitations": [
        "Most experiments use short-answer QA, where alias-based correctness is much easier to evaluate than evidence-grounded long-form generation.",
        "Long-form answers would require explicit evidence attribution and human evaluation, which are not tested.",
        "Measured latency is hardware-specific and based on batch size one; production batching, asynchronous retrieval, and KV-cache reuse can change the break-even point.",
        "The work does not reproduce complete Self-RAG or Adaptive-RAG systems, so those comparisons isolate decision signals rather than full pipelines.",
        "Calibration can drift under domain shift and therefore requires monitoring and likely recalibration.",
        "The method does not model enterprise authorization, document-version constraints, or explicit freshness requirements.",
        "High-confidence closed-book answers can still require mandatory retrieval in safety-, compliance-, or transparency-sensitive settings.",
        "The approach relies on a calibration dataset with correctness labels before deployable thresholds can be selected."
      ],
      "reproducibility": {
        "code_available": true,
        "dataset_available": true,
        "metrics_reported": true
      },
      "confidence_scores": {
        "calibration_improves_probability_quality": 0.99,
        "graded_allocation_saves_passage_budget_not_retrieval_calls": 0.99,
        "retrieval_skip_rate_depends_on_reader_headroom": 0.99,
        "held_out_thresholds_adapt_to_dataset_difficulty": 0.99,
        "chosen_answer_confidence_enables_selective_abstention": 0.97,
        "gating_has_a_real_latency_break_even_point": 0.99,
        "retriever_quality_bounds_gating_benefit": 0.98,
        "domain_shift_requires_recalibration_monitoring": 0.99
      },
      "raw_claims": [
        "The system first estimates the probability that the closed-book answer is correct.",
        "A binary policy chooses between skipping retrieval and retrieving five passages.",
        "A graded policy chooses among zero, one, and five retrieved passages using two calibrated thresholds.",
        "Retrieval-call cost, full-context usage, and passage budget are reported as distinct cost axes.",
        "Retrieving one passage saves context tokens but does not eliminate the retrieval call.",
        "Calibration greatly reduces probability-calibration error for the tested uncertainty signals.",
        "Larger readers can skip substantially more retrieval on TriviaQA while preserving always-RAG accuracy.",
        "When closed-book accuracy is low, validation-selected policies correctly converge toward near-always retrieval.",
        "Selective RAG can abstain when confidence in the answer actually returned is too low.",
        "A separate closed-book probe can make gating slower unless enough queries skip retrieval.",
        "The benefit of adaptive retrieval depends strongly on retriever quality and corpus difficulty.",
        "The study includes a full-Wikipedia stress-test index containing millions of passages.",
        "Code, scripts, prompts, decision tables, label corrections, and archived artifacts are publicly released.",
        "Calibration can become unreliable after domain shift and should be monitored in deployment."
      ],
      "source_url": "https://arxiv.org/html/2606.29959",
      "access": "full_text"
    }
  ],
  "skipped": []
}
